subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Structure and function of the brain
Neurons, synapses and the central nervous system
Key studies: Damasio et al. (1994); Sperry (1968)

questions.q: Which two structures make up the central nervous system (CNS)?
options: The brain and the spinal cord
The brain and the sensory neurons
The spinal cord and the muscles
questions.explain: The CNS is made up of the brain and the spinal cord, which coordinate the body's activity.

questions.q: Which lobe of the brain is mainly responsible for processing visual information?
questions.explain: The occipital lobe, at the back of the brain, contains the visual cortex which processes sight.

questions.q: What is the main function of the cerebellum?
questions.explain: The cerebellum controls balance, muscular coordination and the fine-tuning of movement.

questions.q: What are the three main types of neuron?
questions.explain: The three types are sensory (to the CNS), relay (within the CNS) and motor (from the CNS) neurons.

questions.q: Which structure connects the two hemispheres of the brain?
questions.explain: The corpus callosum is a band of nerve fibres that allows communication between the left and right hemispheres.

questions.q: What type of patients did Sperry (1968) study?
options: Split-brain patients whose corpus callosum had been cut
Patients with damage to the occipital lobe
questions.explain: Sperry studied split-brain patients whose corpus callosum had been severed to treat severe epilepsy.

questions.q: Whose brain injury did Damasio et al. (1994) investigate?
questions.explain: Damasio et al. used Phineas Gage's preserved skull to reconstruct the damage caused by an iron rod passing through his brain.

questions.q: What is a synapse?
options: The long fibre that carries an impulse
The fatty layer around an axon
The control centre of the neuron
questions.explain: A synapse is the tiny gap between neurons across which chemical neurotransmitters are passed.

questions.q: How is a signal passed across the synapse from one neuron to the next?
options: Neurotransmitters are released and cross the gap to the next neuron
An electrical spark jumps directly between the neurons
The axons of the two neurons physically join together
The myelin sheath carries the impulse across the gap
questions.explain: Chemical neurotransmitters are released into the synapse and bind to receptors on the next neuron to pass the signal on.

questions.q: Which functions are most associated with the frontal lobe?
questions.explain: The frontal lobe is involved in higher functions such as reasoning, planning, decision-making and personality.

questions.q: Which side of the body does the left hemisphere of the brain mainly control?
options: The right side of the body
The left side of the body
questions.explain: Control is contralateral, so the left hemisphere controls the right side of the body and vice versa.

questions.q: What is the role of a motor neuron?
options: To carry impulses from the CNS to effectors such as muscles
To carry impulses from receptors to the CNS
To connect sensory and motor neurons within the CNS
To store memories in the brain
questions.explain: Motor neurons carry impulses away from the CNS to effectors (muscles and glands) to produce a response.

questions.q: The thalamus is often described as a 'relay station'. What does this mean?
options: It passes on sensory information to the correct areas of the brain
It produces hormones for the body
It controls automatic functions like breathing
questions.explain: The thalamus receives sensory information and relays it to the appropriate parts of the cerebral cortex.

questions.q: In most people, which hemisphere is language function mainly localised to?
questions.explain: Language areas such as Broca's and Wernicke's areas are usually found in the left hemisphere.

questions.q: What did Damasio et al. (1994) conclude from their study of Phineas Gage?
options: Damage to the frontal lobe affects emotion and decision-making
Damage to the occipital lobe causes blindness
Memory is stored in the cerebellum
questions.explain: They concluded that damage to the frontal (prefrontal) cortex disrupts emotional processing and rational decision-making.

questions.q: What did Sperry (1968) conclude about the two hemispheres of the brain?
options: The two hemispheres have different, specialised functions
The two hemispheres always work in exactly the same way
Only the right hemisphere can process language
The hemispheres cannot function without the cerebellum
questions.explain: Sperry's split-brain findings showed the hemispheres are lateralised, with the left specialised for language and the right for non-verbal tasks.

questions.q: In a Sperry-style task, an object is flashed only to a split-brain patient's left visual field. What is the likely result?
options: The patient cannot name it aloud but can select it by touch with the left hand
The patient can easily name the object aloud
The patient can name it but cannot pick it up
The patient sees nothing at all
questions.explain: The left visual field sends information to the right hemisphere, which lacks language, so the object cannot be named but can be identified by touch with the left hand.

questions.q: A patient suffers damage to the back of their brain and now struggles to process what they see. Which lobe is most likely affected?
questions.explain: The occipital lobe at the back of the brain contains the visual cortex, so damage there impairs vision.

questions.q: A person touches a hot object and quickly pulls their hand away. In what order do neurons carry this signal?
options: Sensory neuron, relay neuron, motor neuron
Motor neuron, relay neuron, sensory neuron
Relay neuron, sensory neuron, motor neuron
Motor neuron, sensory neuron, relay neuron
questions.explain: Sensory neurons carry the signal to the CNS, relay neurons connect within it, and motor neurons carry the response to the muscles.

questions.q: After an accident, a previously calm, reliable worker becomes impulsive and rude, though they can still see, move and speak normally. This pattern is most like which case?
options: Phineas Gage, studied by Damasio et al. (1994)
The split-brain patients studied by Sperry (1968)
A patient with occipital lobe damage
questions.explain: Frontal-lobe damage, as in Phineas Gage, tends to change personality and emotional control while leaving basic senses and movement intact.
